heading: A reactor is a kettle with an unusual firebox
body: Strip away the containment dome and the security fence and a nuclear power station is a steam plant. Heat boils water, steam spins a turbine, the turbine spins a generator, and the generator pushes current onto the grid. The turbine hall of a nuclear station would be recognisable to an engineer from a coal plant of the same vintage, because it is essentially the same machine. Everything distinctive about nuclear power is upstream of the steam, in how the heat is made. In a coal or gas plant, heat comes from a chemical reaction: carbon and hydrogen combining with oxygen, rearranging the outer electrons of atoms. In a reactor it comes from splitting the nucleus itself, and the difference in scale is the whole point. Burning one carbon atom releases about 4 electronvolts. Splitting one uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 million electronvolts — roughly fifty million times more energy from one event. That ratio is why the fuel is measured in tonnes rather than trainloads. A single gram of uranium-235, fully fissioned, yields about a megawatt-day of heat, which is around 23,000 kilowatt-hours, the energy in something like three and a half tonnes of coal. A fuel assembly you could lift with a crane runs a city block for years. The consequence that shapes everything else is that the fuel is small and the waste is small, and because both are small they are concentrated. A coal plant's waste is dispersed up a chimney by the million tonnes and into ash ponds by the hundred thousand; nobody guards it, and its harm is diffuse and statistical. A reactor's waste fits in a room, and it is intensely radioactive. Nuclear power trades a diffuse, unavoidable, continuous harm for a concentrated, containable, occasionally catastrophic one. Almost every argument about the technology is really an argument about whether that is a good trade, and reasonable people weigh concentrated and diffuse risk differently. The second consequence is inertia. Chemical combustion stops when you stop feeding it fuel or air. A reactor's chain reaction stops in about a second when you drop the control rods, but the fuel does not go cold, because the fragments left behind by fission are themselves radioactive and keep decaying whether you want them to or not. That residual heat is the reason a reactor needs cooling long after it has been shut down, and it is the direct cause of the two worst civil accidents in the technology's history. A fire you can put out; a reactor you have to keep cooling. Everything that follows in this guide is an elaboration of those three facts. The energy density is enormous, which makes the fuel cheap and the plant expensive. The material is concentrated, which makes containment both possible and essential. And the heat does not switch off, which is why the engineering is dominated not by making power but by removing heat reliably under every condition anyone has thought of, including the loss of the grid connection the plant is there to serve.

heading: The chain reaction, and the accident of physics that makes it controllable
body: A uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes briefly uranium-236, wobbles, and splits into two lighter nuclei — typically something around krypton and something around barium, though the split is not fixed. It also throws out two or three free neutrons. If, on average, exactly one of those neutrons goes on to cause another fission, the reaction sustains itself at a steady rate. That average is called k, the multiplication factor. At k = 1 the reactor is critical, which in the trade simply means running steadily; it is not a warning word. Below 1 the reaction dies away, above 1 it grows. Natural uranium will not do this on its own in an ordinary reactor. It is 99.3 per cent uranium-238, which absorbs neutrons without usefully fissioning, and only 0.7 per cent uranium-235, which is the isotope that splits. Most reactors therefore run on fuel enriched to between three and five per cent uranium-235. This is worth stating plainly because it is the source of a persistent public confusion: a weapon needs uranium enriched to something like ninety per cent, more than an order of magnitude further along a difficult and conspicuous industrial process. A power reactor's fuel cannot explode like a bomb, and not because of any safety system — the physics simply is not there. Whatever else goes wrong at a nuclear plant, and things do, a nuclear explosion is not on the list. The part that makes control possible at all is a quirk. If every neutron from fission appeared instantly, a reactor would be ungovernable. The average time between one fission and the next it causes is about a ten-thousandth of a second, so a reactor even slightly above critical would double its power faster than any mechanical system could respond, and far faster than any human. But roughly 0.65 per cent of the neutrons from uranium-235 fission are not prompt. They come out of certain unstable fission fragments seconds to minutes after the split that made them. These are the delayed neutrons, and although they are a tiny minority they dominate the timing, because a reactor is operated in the narrow band where it is subcritical on prompt neutrons alone and relies on the delayed ones to close the gap to k = 1. In that band the reactor's response time is set not by ten-thousandths of a second but by the half-lives of those fragments — tens of seconds. Power changes then happen at a pace an operator can watch on a dial and a control system can comfortably manage. Reactor operators call the boundary of that band prompt criticality, and staying below it is the single most important rule in the trade. Chernobyl crossed it. The safety of every civil reactor running today rests, at bottom, on a 0.65 per cent accident of nuclear physics that nobody designed and that happens to be exactly what makes the technology usable.

heading: Moderation: why the neutrons have to be slowed down
body: Neutrons come out of fission fast — around fourteen thousand kilometres per second, carrying a couple of million electronvolts. At that speed they are surprisingly poor at causing further fission. Uranium-235 is far more likely to capture a slow neutron than a fast one; the difference is a factor of hundreds. So a reactor that runs on low-enriched uranium has to slow its neutrons down before they escape or are absorbed uselessly. The material that does this is the moderator, and the choice of moderator is the single biggest fork in reactor design. Slowing a neutron means making it bounce off something. Momentum does the rest: a neutron that hits a heavy nucleus rebounds like a marble off a bowling ball, losing almost nothing, while one that hits a nucleus of about its own mass can lose most of its energy in a single collision. The ideal moderator is therefore made of light nuclei. Hydrogen is the lightest of all, which is why ordinary water is the commonest moderator on earth, and why the phrase "light water reactor" covers the great majority of the world's fleet. Ordinary water has one drawback: hydrogen does not only scatter neutrons, it sometimes absorbs one and becomes deuterium. That loss is why light water reactors need enriched fuel — enrichment buys back the neutrons the moderator eats. Heavy water, in which the hydrogen is already deuterium, has almost no appetite for further neutrons, so a heavy water reactor can run on unenriched natural uranium. Canada's CANDU design does exactly this, which is attractive if you would rather not build an enrichment plant, and comes at the cost of producing heavy water, which is itself expensive. Graphite is the third classic choice: carbon is heavier than hydrogen so it takes more collisions, but it absorbs almost nothing, and it is a solid that tolerates high temperatures. Britain's gas-cooled reactors and the Soviet RBMK both used it. The moderator choice cascades into everything. It sets the enrichment you need, which sets the fuel supply chain. It sets whether the coolant and moderator are the same substance, which sets what happens when you lose the coolant. And that last point is where the deepest safety property of the common designs lives. In a light water reactor, water is both moderator and coolant. Lose the water, or let it boil into steam, and you lose the moderation — the neutrons stay fast, fission falls off, and the chain reaction shuts itself down. The reactor's response to losing its coolant is to stop reacting. This is called a negative void coefficient, and it is not a system that can fail; it is a property of the physics, active whether or not anyone is awake. A graphite-moderated, water-cooled design does not have it, because losing the water removes a neutron absorber while leaving the moderator in place. The RBMK at Chernobyl was of that kind, and at low power its void coefficient was positive: boiling made it more reactive, not less. That is the difference between a design whose physics argues with an accident and one whose physics joins in.

heading: Control: rods, boron, and the feedback that does most of the work
body: Control rods are the part everyone can picture: neutron-hungry metal on a shaft, driven into the core to soak up neutrons and stop the reaction, withdrawn to let it run. The materials are chosen for appetite — boron, usually as boron carbide, and cadmium, hafnium and silver-indium-cadmium alloys. Dropping them all in is called a scram or a trip, and it takes a couple of seconds. In most designs gravity does it, and the electromagnets that hold the rods up release when power is lost, so a station blackout drops the rods rather than stranding them. Failing towards shutdown is a principle, not a coincidence. Rods are the coarse instrument. Pressurised water reactors also carry boron dissolved in the coolant itself — chemical shim — whose concentration is trimmed slowly over weeks to track the fuel's gradual burn-up. That leaves the rods free for fine adjustment and emergency use rather than being constantly worked. Boiling water reactors, which cannot use soluble boron in normal operation because the boiling would concentrate it unevenly, instead vary the flow of coolant through the core: push more water through and you get less steam, more moderation and more power. It is control by pump rather than by chemistry. But the control that matters most is not operated by anyone. Two feedback effects act on the fuel directly, in milliseconds, without instruction. The first is the Doppler effect in uranium-238. As fuel heats up, the nuclei in it jiggle faster, which smears out the energies at which uranium-238 absorbs neutrons and widens its capture bands. A hotter core therefore eats more of its own neutrons. Power rises, temperature rises, absorption rises, power falls. It is a thermostat built into the fuel pellets, it responds as fast as the fuel heats, and there is nothing to fail. The second is the void and temperature coefficient of the moderator described earlier: in a light water reactor, hotter and less dense water moderates less well, so power falls. Between them these two effects mean a properly designed light water core resists its own excursions. An operator error that would send an unstable design running away is instead met, within a fraction of a second, by physics pushing back. This is why the language of "safety systems" undersells modern reactor safety and, oddly, undermines confidence in it. Systems can fail, and people rightly discount them. The Doppler coefficient is not a system. Designers speak of defence in depth — the fuel's own feedback, then the cladding, then the pressure vessel, then the containment building, then the emergency cooling, then the site's exclusion zone — and the innermost layer, the one that acts first and never needs power, is not built at all. It is chosen, at the design stage, by picking a core whose physics is on your side.

heading: The pressurised water reactor, and why most of the world runs one
body: Around two-thirds of the world's power reactors are pressurised water reactors, and the design's dominance is more historical accident than considered choice: it descends from the compact reactor Admiral Rickover's programme developed for American submarines in the early 1950s, which needed to be small, tolerate a boat that pitches and rolls, and never boil in a hull full of sailors. Scaled up and put ashore, it became the industry's default. The trick in the name is that the water is kept under enough pressure not to boil. The primary circuit runs at about 155 bar — roughly 150 times atmospheric pressure — which raises water's boiling point past 340 °C. Coolant enters the core near 290 °C and leaves near 325 °C, hot enough to be useful, still liquid throughout. Keeping it liquid matters: liquid water carries heat far better than steam, and a core that never boils has no boiling to go wrong. That hot water does not go anywhere near the turbine. It flows to a steam generator, a vessel full of thousands of thin U-shaped tubes, and gives its heat through the tube walls to a completely separate secondary circuit at lower pressure, which does boil. The secondary steam drives the turbine, condenses, and returns. The two circuits touch only through metal. The point of that separation is that anything radioactive stays in the primary loop, inside containment, so the turbine hall is an ordinary industrial space that people walk through in overalls. It also means a leak in a steam generator tube is a serious event, because it is the one place where the two circuits are close enough to fail into each other. A pressuriser — a tall vessel part full of steam, with heaters and a cold-water spray — sits on the primary loop and holds the pressure steady, absorbing the expansion and contraction of the coolant as power changes. It is the shock absorber of the system, and its relief valve was the component that stuck open at Three Mile Island. The reactor vessel itself is a steel forging with walls of the order of twenty centimetres thick, holding a core of a couple of hundred fuel assemblies, each a bundle of a few hundred slender zirconium-alloy tubes packed with uranium dioxide pellets. Around all of it stands the containment: a steel-lined, prestressed concrete structure typically about a metre thick, designed to hold the pressure of the entire primary circuit flashing to steam, and incidentally to survive an aircraft impact. The design's virtues are its separation of circuits, its strongly negative feedback, and half a century of accumulated operating experience across hundreds of units. Its vices are that everything runs at very high pressure, which makes the vessel and piping enormous and expensive engineering; and that thermal efficiency is only around 33 to 35 per cent, well below a modern gas plant, because the steam is limited to what pressurised water can deliver. Two-thirds of the heat goes into a river, the sea, or a cooling tower.

heading: Boiling water, heavy water, gas and the designs that took another road
body: The boiling water reactor is the pressurised design's obvious simplification: if the steam has to be made anyway, why not make it in the core? A BWR runs at about 75 bar, lets the water boil among the fuel, and pipes the steam straight to the turbine. Out go the steam generators, the pressuriser and the second circuit; the pressure vessel is larger but the plant is simpler and thermally much the same. The price is that the turbine now handles slightly radioactive steam, mostly from nitrogen-16 produced in the coolant, so the turbine hall is a controlled area during operation. Nitrogen-16 has a seven-second half-life, so the hall is safe to enter shortly after shutdown, but you cannot wander in mid-shift. BWRs also control power partly by coolant flow, which gives them a smooth response to load changes. CANDU, the Canadian deuterium-uranium design, takes the heavy water road. Because heavy water barely absorbs neutrons, it runs on natural uranium, sidestepping enrichment entirely. Instead of one big pressure vessel it uses hundreds of horizontal pressure tubes running through a tank of cool heavy water moderator, and that geometry allows refuelling while the reactor is at full power, pushing fresh bundles in one end and spent ones out the other. High availability is the reward. The drawbacks are the cost of heavy water, a positive void coefficient requiring careful design compensation, and the fact that on-load refuelling is exactly the capability that makes a reactor useful for producing weapons-grade plutonium, which has made the design politically sensitive to export. Britain went its own way twice. The Magnox reactors and their successors, the advanced gas-cooled reactors, use graphite as moderator and carbon dioxide as coolant, blowing gas at high pressure through channels in a graphite stack. Gas cooling allows much higher outlet temperatures — around 640 °C in an AGR — and therefore thermal efficiency above 40 per cent, the best of any commercial reactor type. The cost was engineering complexity, difficult construction and a fleet that was expensive to build and never exported. The Soviet RBMK combined graphite moderation with water cooling in pressure tubes, was cheap, could be built very large and refuelled on load, and had the positive void coefficient discussed earlier. The surviving units were substantially modified after 1986, and the type has been progressively retired. Fast reactors — sodium-cooled, unmoderated — are the road most often taken and least often finished. Without a moderator, fast neutrons can convert uranium-238 into plutonium faster than the plutonium is consumed, breeding more fuel than they burn and, in principle, extending uranium reserves by a factor of many tens. France, Russia, Japan, the United States and India have all built them; sodium, which burns in air and reacts violently with water, has made them difficult to operate reliably, and only Russia currently runs them commercially at scale. Small modular reactors are the current wave: factory-built units of tens to a few hundred megawatts, trucked to site, betting that serial production beats bespoke construction. The argument is economic rather than nuclear. Whether it is right is not yet settled by anything built and operating commercially in the West.

heading: Decay heat: the problem that does not switch off
body: Drop the control rods and fission stops within about a second. The reactor does not. The fission fragments accumulated in the fuel — iodine, caesium, strontium, xenon and a long tail of others — are unstable, and they go on decaying on their own schedules, releasing heat regardless of what the rods are doing. Immediately after shutdown this decay heat is about six to seven per cent of the reactor's full thermal power. For a large reactor producing three gigawatts of heat, that is around two hundred megawatts — the output of a decent-sized gas turbine, appearing inside a core that has just been shut down, with nobody able to turn it off. It falls away, but slowly and on a stubborn curve. After an hour it is around one per cent; after a day, a few tenths of a per cent; after a year, still enough that spent fuel must be actively cooled. Ten megawatts of unremovable heat in a sealed vessel is more than enough to boil the coolant away, uncover the fuel, and destroy it. This single fact is the organising problem of reactor safety, and understanding it explains why nuclear plants look the way they do. Multiple independent cooling trains, each able to do the job alone. Emergency core cooling that injects water under pressure. Diesel generators, usually several, to run the pumps when the grid is gone — and the grid is very often gone, because whatever knocked the plant offline may well have knocked the transmission out too. Batteries to bridge the minutes before the diesels start. Passive systems in newer designs that circulate coolant by natural convection and dump heat to a tank of water sitting above the reactor, needing no pump and no power at all, sometimes for three days unattended. Both of the accidents that destroyed reactor cores were decay-heat accidents. At Three Mile Island a relief valve stuck open, coolant escaped, and operators — misreading their instruments — throttled back the emergency injection that was doing exactly what it should. The chain reaction had stopped as designed; decay heat uncovered and melted about half the core anyway. At Fukushima Daiichi the reactors scrammed correctly on the earthquake, and then the tsunami flooded the emergency diesel generators, which were sited low. The plant lost the grid, then lost its backup power, and with it the ability to remove a heat load that would not stop. Cores melted over the following days. Neither accident involved a runaway chain reaction. Both were failures to remove heat from a reactor that was already shut down. That is the distinctive hazard of the technology, and it is why the correct question to ask of any reactor design is not "how does it stop?" — they all stop — but "how does it stay cool with no power, no operators and no water supply, and for how long?"
